title: The Compass of the Empty Quarter
premise: Astrid Ashgrove, a nonbinary railroad surveyor who has spent a decade erasing themselves into schedules and gradients, salvages a sealed chest from a flooded river bend—stamped with the crest of Vharska, a nation that no longer exists. Inside are survey maps of closed lines and a ledger naming officials who sold an entire border region's people into forced labor before the state dissolved. When Astrid realizes one of those names belongs to the magnate now funding their own railway commission, they must decide whether to bury the chest again or carry its evidence across three hundred miles of empty quarter to the last living witness—a former clerk hiding in a desert station town—before the magnate's private security closes the line for good. Astrid delivers the ledger, but at the cost of their anonymity: justice outside the law requires standing in the open, and Astrid ends the book testifying under their own name, finally measured in years instead of miles.
about_author: Xanthe Galloway is a former freight-line dispatcher who writes adventure fiction from a converted signal box on the edge of the moors. Their work explores what people owe each other when every official system has failed them.

chapters.title: The River Keeps Its Accounts
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. During a routine flood-season inspection of a decommissioned spur, Astrid's crew unearths a lead-lined chest stamped with Vharska's extinct seal. Astrid, who values invisibility above all, orders it quietly logged as scrap—but pockets the key. Emotional beat: unease; the past has a weight that doesn't fit on any survey sheet.

chapters.title: Miles, Not Years
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, with flashback fragments to ten years earlier, when Astrid fled a small-town scandal by taking a nameless job on the rails. We learn why Astrid measures life in miles and trusts timetables over people. The chapter closes with Astrid alone at night, turning the strange key over. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for safety.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Names
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In a locked hotel room, Astrid opens the chest: maps of lines that officially never existed, and a ledger of Vharskan officials who profited from deportations along the border corridor. One signature matches Halvard Crane, the industrialist whose money built Astrid's own commission. Emotional beat: vertigo—the map of Astrid's career is drawn over someone else's crime.

chapters.title: The Man Who Buys Rivers
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Crane learns a salvage crew pulled something from the Kessel bend and dispatches his security chief, Maren Voss, to 'assist' the railway commission. We see his charm, his ledgers, and his genuine belief that history is a debt he's already paid off. Emotional beat: cold dread; the reader knows the hunter before the prey does.

chapters.title: Voss Comes Aboard
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Voss joins the survey team under cover of an insurance audit, asking precise questions about the river bend. Astrid lies smoothly for the first time in ten years and hates how easily it comes. A young crew member, Tomas, notices the chest is missing from the log. Emotional beat: paranoia tightening like a coupler under strain.

chapters.title: The Empty Quarter
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid and Voss POVs. Astrid slips away at night with the chest aboard a handcar, heading across the closed desert lines toward Station Nine, where records say the last Vharskan clerk, Ilya Brandt, still lives. Voss finds the empty bunk and gives chase along the same rails. Emotional beat: exhilaration curdling into fear—the open country offers no cover.

chapters.title: Station Nine
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid finds Brandt, old and bitter, keeping a dying water tower alive out of habit. He refuses the ledger at first—he buried his own name decades ago and survived by forgetting. Only when Astrid admits their own reasons for hiding does he agree to sign a sworn statement. Emotional beat: two exiles recognizing each other across a generation.

chapters.title: The Last Train Through
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, then Astrid's. Voss's men seal the line behind Astrid; Brandt's statement must leave on the one scheduled freight train, and Voss controls the junction. Astrid reroutes the train through a condemned tunnel using the dead nation's own secret maps—knowledge only a railroad engineer could weaponize. Emotional beat: triumph with a price tag attached.

chapters.title: Junction at Kessel Bend
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Confrontation at the flooded crossing where it all began: Voss offers Astrid silence, promotion, a clean new name—the exact currency Astrid has traded in for a decade. Astrid refuses, choosing exposure over erasure, and buys time for the statement to reach a journalist and a tribunal clerk. Emotional beat: the climax of identity—choosing to be seen.

chapters.title: Measured in Years
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, months later. The tribunal opens; Crane falls, not spectacularly but irreversibly, the way empires actually do. Astrid testifies under their full name, hands shaking, and walks out into a crowd that now knows them. The chest goes to a museum; the maps go back to the descendants of the deported. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace—invisibility was never safety, and being known is survivable.
